name: O'Connell Monument
historical_description: Bronze monument to Daniel O'Connell, conceived by John Henry Foley in 1866 and completed by Thomas Brock in 1883. It includes a high-relief frieze and multiple figures around a granite plinth.
historical_significance: Major national monument at the southern entrance to O'Connell Street.

name: Central Hall, 71 Clontarf Road — 1906 Methodist hall
historical_description: Attached Methodist hall built in 1906, with a gabled south façade and a link block connecting it to the associated church. NIAH records a natural-slate roof, cast-iron rainwater goods, cut-granite verge stones and carved kneelers, crenellated parapet, rusticated granite walls and plinth, stained-glass pointed-arch windows, granite door surrounds, steps and threshold. The front elevation carries an inscribed sandstone plaque reading “Central Hall 1906”.
historical_significance: A documented early twentieth-century Methodist hall associated with an earlier church on the site (1867, extended 1881). NIAH attributes the 1906 hall to the builders Collen Brothers and the designs of W.M. Mitchell and Sons. The building preserves a legible date inscription and crafted granite and stained-glass details.
access_status: Hall and adjoining church have managed/private access. Photograph exterior from public footpath where visible; obtain permission before entering grounds or photographing interiors. Do not obstruct the footpath.

name: Clontarf Castle gate lodge — Gothic Revival entrance building
address: Entrance to Clontarf Castle, Castle Avenue, Clontarf, Dublin 3
historical_description: Detached complex-plan gate lodge built in 1836–37, comprising a three-bay, two-storey building with a three-stage round tower, gabled bay containing a former carriage arch, carved limestone spire and crenellated elements. NIAH records carved limestone coping, stringcourses, corbel table with sculpted animal heads, stepped buttresses, shield over the former carriage arch, pointed-arch openings, carved hood-mouldings, cut-limestone mullions and granite bollards linked by steel chains.
historical_significance: A richly detailed Gothic Revival gate lodge associated with Clontarf Castle. NIAH attributes the rebuilding to designs by William Vitruvius Morrison and notes that early Ordnance Survey maps show the avenue passing through the Tudor arch. The sculpted animal heads and carved limestone details are evidence of nineteenth-century stonemasonry.
access_status: At the entrance to Clontarf Castle Hotel, beside a road roundabout and private hotel grounds. Photograph only from a lawful, safe public viewpoint; do not enter hotel grounds or stand on the carriageway/roundabout without permission.
